passage:
Pankaj, fourteen, sat in the school counsellor's room, arms wrapped around his middle.
"Your stomach again?" Gurleen Ma'am asked.
"It's nothing. Papa says I'm doing drama to skip school." His voice cracked. "So I stopped telling him."
She didn't laugh or doubt him. "Pain is real even when tests don't show a cause. How long has it been happening?"
"Since the new term. Mostly mornings."
"Thank you for telling me. I'm going to call your parents today and suggest a proper check with a doctor, so we know your body is okay. And then, if you want, we can talk about what mornings feel like."
Pankaj looked up. "You believe me?"
"I do."
That evening his mother took him to the clinic. And on Thursday, Pankaj came back to Gurleen Ma'am's room and talked about how scared he'd been of the new class.

qa.q: When does Pankaj's stomach pain mostly happen?
qa.a: Mostly in the mornings, since the new term.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel when Papa called it drama?
qa.a: He felt hurt and unheard, so he stopped telling Papa about the pain.

qa.q: How did Gurleen Ma'am open the way for Pankaj to talk?
qa.a: She believed him, called his parents that day to arrange a doctor's check, and offered to talk about his mornings when he was ready.

qa.q: How might Pankaj's mother have felt after Gurleen Ma'am's call?
qa.a: She was probably concerned enough to act, since she took him to the clinic that very evening.

grounding: It shows a teenager whose pain was dismissed as attention-seeking hiding his distress, and how taking the symptoms seriously opens the way to talking about stress.

passage:
Dear Papa,

Mumma says I should write this down because I get tongue-tied when I try to say it, so here it is.
Last Sunday, when I said my head hurt again, you said, "Enough drama, Sunaina, you just don't want to study." I know you were tired. But it really hurt, Papa. Not just my head. That you didn't believe me.
Since then I've been hiding it. I take my books to the terrace so you won't see me rubbing my forehead. Some days I feel dizzy and I still don't say anything.
I'm not trying to get out of studying. I think maybe I'm stressed about the board exams, and my body is showing it. Can we please go to the doctor to check? And after that, can we talk?

Love,
Sunaina

P.S. Mumma says, "Sahil, read it twice."

qa.q: Where does Sunaina take the books to hide the pain?
qa.a: Sunaina takes the books to the terrace.

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel when Papa called it drama?
qa.a: Sunaina felt hurt and disbelieved, which hurt even more than the headache.

qa.q: What does Sunaina ask for, and why is it a good step?
qa.a: A doctor's check and then a talk, because taking the pain seriously could also open up the stress about the board exams.

qa.q: How might Papa feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Papa might feel sorry and surprised to learn that those words made Sunaina hide the pain and dizziness.

grounding: It shows a teenager whose headaches were dismissed as drama feeling unheard and hiding distress, and asking for the symptoms to be checked and the stress talked about.
